After spinal injury, random act of kindness 'blesses' D.M. family (article pasted in comments to avoid ad)

On an unseasonably warm March afternoon last year, Darin Stevenson was building a playhouse for his kids. But this wasn’t just any playhouse.

An engineer by trade, Darin built a two-story, tricked-out work of art with a climbing wall, hallways, hiding places, big slides and a zip line.

He was securing that zip line while standing at the top of a 15-foot ladder when he fell and suffered a life-threatening spinal cord injury. In the few moments of clarity he had before he passed out, he told his wife, Erika Stevenson, to call 911. Soon after, the family realized Darin Stevenson couldn’t move his legs.

In an instant, their life changed, Erika Stevenson said Tuesday. And in the year since the injury, the family — including children Lucy, 8, Colin, 6 and Nora, 2 — has experienced some of their darkest days, but they’ve also been exposed to the brightest parts of humanity.

“People have been so extremely giving with their time,” she said. “People have just gone out of their way to help however they could.”

The family was “blessed” by another random act of kindness last week when an anonymous donor gifted Darin Stevenson $1,000 worth of personal training sessions at the Walnut Creek Y. Erika Stevenson took to Facebook to thank the donor, and her post went viral, getting shared more than 600 times.

“I was overcome with gratitude to the point of tears,” Erika Stevenson said of the gift. “It’s been over a year (since the injury) and there is a point where, as a family, you realize you just need to plod along in your new normal, so we just weren’t expecting this kind of an extra boost.”

Darin Stevenson, who spent 40 days in and out of consciousness at the hospital and months in rehab in Des Moines and Chicago, eventually regained feeling in some parts of his leg, a miracle Erika Stevenson attributes to almost daily exercise.

In pursuit of regaining even more motion, Darin Stevenson made an appointment with a wellness coach at the Walnut Creek Y a few weeks ago to inquire about the best ways to work out and maybe even schedule some personal training sessions.

“You have to realize Darin looks different,” Erika Stevenson said. “He’s a 40-year-old guy walking around with two canes and a pad on his butt in case he falls. He looks different than other Y members, and someone noticed him and inquired about the story.”

That person, who wishes to remain anonymous, then bought 20 sessions, a $1,000 value, and gifted them to Darin. (With medical bills and three children, the sessions are not something the Stevensons could have afforded on their own.)

“It had all of us staff members really choked up,” said Britt German, executive director of the Walnut Creek Y. “We strive so hard to make sure we are serving the community, and to have a member go above and beyond with this random act of kindness, it’s just emotional for us.”

But this gift was far from the first "random act of kindness" the family has experienced.

In addition to countless warm meals, Darin Stevenson’s former workplace, Des Moines Area Community College, organized “work days” for co-workers to help in the family's backyard. And a group of continuing education students built a mobility ramp from the driveway to the front door.

Both Darin and his wife are sure he wouldn’t be as far into his recovery without the help of this bevy of Good Samaritans.

“There were plenty of moments that Darin was feeling hopeless,” Erika Stevenson said, “and a card would come or someone would hand him a check for $20 or he’d get a text and, in that moment, it was exactly what he needed to persevere.”

A random act of kindness is almost a misnomer for these types of small charities, she said. These are random acts that change lives.

And, she stressed, the point is not the amount of the donation. Not many people can afford to give away $1,000, but a kind word is free.

“Small actions matter,” she said. “You never know the impact they will have, and we are living proof that even the smallest action can have the greatest impact.”
